David Yosuanto 8 min read · Nov 3, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share Why Systems Thinking Implementation Stalls at the Map Systems thinking is mostly used to understand problems, rarely to change them. A four-part test ties every systems map to a decision before anyone draws it. If your organisation has run a systems-thinking exercise in the last two years, you probably still have the artefact: a causal loop diagram, a dozen reinforcing and balancing loops, and one leverage point circled in a different colour. The workshop may well have been the most honest conversation the team had all quarter. The question worth asking now is what that map changed. That question is uncomfortable because the map is usually treated as the hard part. The DG Cities guide to Behavioural Systems Mapping makes the standard case: linear approaches often fail because they treat complex problems as isolated issues, while systems thinking recognises how the parts interact. The assumption that rides along is that once the leverage point is on the wall, change follows. I’d push back on that, because the evidence on how systems thinking is actually used says the work mostly stops at the map. A 2025 INET Oxford review of 27 systems-thinking projects run by or for UK government found 22 used for strategy, 11 used to evaluate policy and only 5 touching execution and implementation, since one project could serve several stages. None was designed only to inform execution, and just 3 of the 27 projects were themselves formally evaluated. Key takeaways Systems thinking in UK environmental policy stays at the front of the process: of 27 projects reviewed by INET Oxford, 22 supported strategy, 5 touched implementation and only 3 were formally evaluated. Systems-change guides spell out mapping but not acting on a map: 42 of 46 guides reviewed by Boston College include a mapping phase, yet none of their five common phases is dedicated to implementation and their evaluation advice rarely offers operational detail. Systems-thinking projects in UK policy were helped by being “hooked into existing asks”, according to interviews by INET Oxford, and analysts rarely embraced the method when deadlines demanded traditional or economic-only outputs. I propose a map-to-decision test for systems maps: before commissioning one, write down the decision it should change, who owns that decision, the feedback loop with its metric and review date, and the result that kills the intervention. A systems map that cannot name the decision it is meant to change should go back to scoping instead of into a presentation. Pete Barbrook-Johnson, Domenica Cox and Alexandra Penn at INET Oxford combined a semi-systematic review of grey and academic literature with interviews of researchers and policymakers. By far the most common objective was building an understanding of a policy area, and they found “a noticeable lack of more targeted or instrumental objectives directly linked to informing particular processes or decisions.” Local operational teams often found the work too strategic and time-consuming, and participants put it bluntly: “people see it [as] too far away from action”. The authors conclude that systems thinking is perceived as an exploratory tool and, “in some cases, as a luxury.” The authors attach their own warning. Their sample leans towards successful projects and organisations open to the method, so in their words “things are likely less positive than they might appear.” Even so, interviewees told them they “don’t think we could say, just for sure, doing this exercise has improved the strategy compared to if you hadn’t done the exercise.” I’d argue it is the same failure as an AI pilot that never crosses into infrastructure inside a product org : the exploratory work is real, and nobody owns the next step. Why do systems-change guides say so little about acting on the map? Because acting on a map is the part they leave least specified. Emily Gates and colleagues at Boston College reviewed 46 practical systems-change guides published between 2014 and 2025, in Systems Research and Behavioral Science. Mapping systems appeared in 42 of them (91%), and so did finding leverage. None of the five phases they synthesise is dedicated to implementation; acting is folded into finding leverage and into learning and adapting. On evaluation, the guides “rarely offer operational detail”. The review’s own diagram of the five phases shows the gap: each one has a label and an icon, and none is labelled for implementation. The pentagon names the five phases the review found across the guides: Explore the Situation and Envision Change, Map Systems, Find Leverage, Navigate Futures, and Learn and Adapt. The review reports them in 45, 42, 42, 17 and 38 of the 46 guides respectively. Acting on the map has no phase of its own. Source:
